svg.text: Process Data — What It Does and Why It Is Needed
up_ProcessAllDataV2 — WarehouseLOC / LoanTracking
1 Why it is needed
The gap a normal business day leaves
• A loan or wire is only recalculated when someone saves it.
• Interest accrues every day regardless of user activity.
• Fees come due on their own schedule, not on user action.
• Curtailments and credit line balances move with time.
• Anything nobody touched that day drifts out of date.
What Process Data does about it
• Sweeps every credit line and every loan — touched or not.
• Recomputes interest, fees, curtailment and balances.
• Brings the whole book to one consistent as-of date.
• Advances LastDayProcessed on the Originator record.
• At month-end, triggers the close and updates history.
2 How it runs
up_ProcessAllDataV2 @ID, @TD, @UserName
Read @LDP = LastDayProcessed, @LPC = LastPeriodClosed
Guards — exit before doing any work
Last Period Close mismatch → RETURN -1 Future date → RETURN -1
DISABLE TRIGGER ALL ON [dbo].[Loan]
Freeze @TD; rewind @LDP back to the 1st of the month
WHILE @LDP <= @TD — day-by-day loop
for each credit line @CLID
WHILE next MIN(LoanID) — loan cursor
up_ProcessLoanDataV2
interest accrual, fees, Over21, rate logic for one loan
up_ProcessParticipation
writes TotalParticipation for the day
Month-end check
IF DAY(DATEADD(day,1,@LDP)) = 1 → up_ProcessMonthEndDataV2
ENABLE TRIGGER ALL ON [dbo].[Loan]
advance LastDayProcessed / LastPeriodClosed
up_ProcessMonthEndDataV2
• Writes LoanHistory and CreditLineHistory
keyed on the period end date: updates the
row if it exists, inserts only when new.
• Averages TotalParticipation across the
month for the NonUsedFee threshold.
• This is the definitive month-end snapshot
— it should be written once, from final data.
Reading the structure
Three nested levels of iteration:
every day in the month
× every credit line
× every loan
@LDP is rewound to the 1st of the month
on every run, so a run on the 31st repeats
the whole month's work — not just today's.
The guards and the trigger disable/enable
bracket the entire operation, so the Loan
table sits with triggers off for the full
duration of the run.
The month-end branch is a condition inside
the day loop, not a separate job.
3 Why it is slow
Row-by-row, not set-based
• Loans are walked one at a time with a MIN(LoanID)
WHILE cursor rather than processed as a set.
• That cursor sits inside a credit line loop, which sits
inside a day loop — cost multiplies across all three.
• Triggers are disabled on Loan for the whole run, so the
table is effectively held for the duration.
• This is the same work the old save path invoked on every
UI save — the cause of the 10–15 second saves, timeouts,
IIS recycling and deadlocks.
The day loop is provably redundant
• Each iteration overwrites the previous one rather
than accumulating, so only the final iteration's
output survives.
• The rate lookup uses a static variable rather than
the loop counter — every iteration reads the same
rate regardless of the day being processed.
• Business confirmed rates change monthly, not
mid-month, so the extra iterations change nothing.
4 How it is triggered — and the schedule problem
Today
• Triggered manually, in the morning.
• Has been run on the last day of the
month being closed.
• Month-end therefore fires against the
morning position, not final data.
Fixed
• Close fires when the loop reaches the
1st of the following month.
• The period end date passed is the last
day of the month being closed.
• All data is final before history is written.
Still open
• A manual trigger means the schedule
depends on someone choosing the
right day.
• Scheduling the job would remove
that dependency.
Simplified for a general audience. Guard conditions, variable handling and error paths are abbreviated — see the procedure for exact logic.
